claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC structure.
The stability of the high-temperature BCC phase in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by thermodynamically driven chemical ordering.
Al–Cr and Al–Ni pairs have strongly negative mixing enthalpies.
Preferential Al–Cr and Al–Ni interactions drive local elemental ordering and nucleation of ordered phases.
Slow cooling or annealing enables diffusion and transforms the metastable BCC phase toward an equilibrium mixture containing ordered precipitates.
Rapid cooling kinetically suppresses chemical ordering and preserves the BCC structure.
Pre-deformation introduces defects that promote nucleation and growth during phase transformation.
Pre-deformed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 should transform with a lower effective activation energy than undeformed material.
Pre-deformed samples should develop a larger fraction of ordered phases than undeformed, rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled or annealed samples should exhibit new ordered phases or distinct precipitates replacing or coexisting with the initial BCC phase.
The predicted precipitates should be enriched in Al together with Cr or Ni.
A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 sample retains the high-temperature BCC phase because ordering is kinetically suppressed.
The proposed transformation occurs only under thermal conditions where atomic diffusion is significant.
Extremely rapid cooling prevents manifestation of the predicted ordered phases.
Temperatures well above the BCC stability limit do not produce the predicted ordered phases.
Very long annealing could cause complete homogenization or additional transformations.
The exact identity, morphology, volume fraction, and Cr-versus-Ni contributions of the ordered phases are not yet quantified.
Failure of slow cooling, annealing, or pre-deformation to produce systematic ordering, segregation, or phase changes relative to the quenched control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism presents diffusion-enabled ordering and precipitation as movement toward equilibrium, whereas the boundary states that sufficiently long annealing could produce complete homogenization. Without specifying a temperature-dependent reversal or another mechanism, homogenization conflicts with the proposed equilibrium tendency toward partitioning and ordered phases.
